questions.question: A specimen is viewed through a 10x eyepiece and a 40x objective lens. The overall magnification of the image is:
questions.explanation: Total magnification is the product of the eyepiece and objective magnifications: 10 × 40 = 400x. Adding the powers gives the wrong 50x, and 100x or 4000x arise from miscalculation.

questions.question: Enlarging an image beyond what the objective can resolve, for example by fitting a stronger eyepiece, mainly produces:
options: A larger, blurrier image with no added detail
Separate images of points that were too close to resolve
A higher numerical aperture in the objective lens
A shorter effective wavelength of the light used
questions.explanation: Resolution is fixed by the objective and the wavelength of light, so magnification beyond that limit is empty magnification: the image grows but no new detail appears. It cannot raise the NA (C) or shorten the wavelength (D).

questions.question: Which change would reduce the smallest distance that a light microscope can resolve, and so improve its resolution?
options: Switching from blue light to red light
Using an objective with a lower numerical aperture
Raising the eyepiece power from 10x to 15x
Switching from red light to blue light
questions.explanation: In d = 0.61λNA a shorter wavelength lowers d. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, so switching red → blue improves resolution. Eyepiece power (C) and a lower NA (B) do not help, and red light is worse than blue (A).

questions.question: Using d = 0.61λNA, the smallest resolvable distance for light of wavelength 550 nm and an objective of numerical aperture 1.25 is closest to:
questions.explanation: d = 0.61 × 550 nm ÷ 1.25 ≈ 268 nm. The value 336 nm omits the division by NA, and 440 nm omits the 0.61 factor.

questions.question: Immersion oil is placed between the slide and the 100x objective mainly because it:
options: Cools the specimen by absorbing lamp heat
Stops light bending away, so more rays enter the lens
Extends the working distance of the objective
Raises contrast by faintly staining the specimen
questions.explanation: Oil has a refractive index close to that of glass, so oblique rays are not refracted out of the lens path. This raises the effective numerical aperture and resolution. It does not cool the specimen (A), extend working distance (C), or stain (D).

questions.question: When the objective is changed from 10x to 40x, the depth of field generally:
options: Increases because the image becomes larger
Stays the same because the eyepiece is unchanged
Increases because the working distance shortens
Decreases because the numerical aperture rises
questions.explanation: Higher-power objectives have higher numerical aperture, which gives a thinner zone of the specimen that is in focus at one time — so the depth of field decreases.

questions.question: A microscope has a field of view 1.8 mm across at a total magnification of 100x. At 400x total magnification the field diameter is:
questions.explanation: Field diameter is inversely proportional to magnification, so 1.8 mm × 100400 = 0.45 mm.

questions.question: The numerical aperture of an objective lens depends on:
options: Eyepiece focal length and tube length
Wavelength of light and stage height
Refractive index of the medium and half-angle of the light cone collected
questions.explanation: NA = n sin θ, so it is set by the refractive index of the medium between specimen and lens and by the half-angle of the cone of light the lens accepts.

questions.question: The condenser of a compound light microscope mainly serves to:
options: Focus lamp light into a cone that illuminates the specimen
Magnify the real image formed by the objective
Hold the objectives on a revolving turret
Fine-adjust the distance between stage and objective
questions.explanation: The condenser gathers and concentrates light from the source onto the specimen, which affects brightness and resolution. Magnification (B) is the job of the objective and eyepiece.

questions.question: Partly closing the condenser iris diaphragm when viewing a stained smear generally:
options: Improves resolution while dimming the image
Raises resolution and depth of field together
Changes magnification but leaves contrast the same
Raises contrast and depth of field but lowers resolution
questions.explanation: A smaller aperture lowers the illuminating NA, which increases contrast and depth of field but reduces resolving power.

questions.question: Objectives on a microscope are described as parfocal when:
options: They all give the same magnification
The specimen stays almost in focus after switching objectives
They share the same numerical aperture
questions.explanation: Parfocal objectives are matched in focal distance so that only slight refocusing is needed when the nosepiece is rotated.

questions.question: Köhler illumination is set up in order to provide:
options: The highest magnification the objective allows
Even, glare-free illumination across the whole field of view
A longer working distance at high power
questions.explanation: Köhler alignment focuses and centres the condenser and field diaphragm so the lamp filament is not imaged and light is uniform and glare-free.

questions.question: After focusing a stained smear with the 10x objective on a parfocal microscope, the correct way to sharpen the image at 40x is to use:
options: The coarse focus knob with the stage raised
The fine focus knob in small adjustments
The iris diaphragm to bring the specimen into focus
questions.explanation: Parfocal objectives need only slight refocusing, and the coarse knob risks driving the lens into the slide. Use the fine focus knob in small adjustments.

questions.question: Coloured fringes around an image arise because different wavelengths are focused at different points. This defect is called:
questions.explanation: A simple lens refracts shorter wavelengths more strongly than longer ones, so colours do not converge at a single focus — this is chromatic aberration.

questions.question: Which objective class gives the most complete correction of chromatic aberration (at three wavelengths) and of spherical aberration, at the highest cost?
questions.explanation: Apochromats use special glass and complex lens groups to correct colour at three wavelengths, whereas achromats correct only two.

questions.question: Which specimen is best viewed by dark-field microscopy?
questions.explanation: Dark-field illumination makes thin, unstained live organisms such as spirochaetes appear bright against a dark background, since they are too slender for bright-field.

questions.question: Phase-contrast microscopy makes transparent, unstained cells visible by converting differences in which property into differences in brightness?
options: Rotation of the plane of polarised light
Phase shift caused by refractive index and thickness
questions.explanation: Light passing through parts of a cell with different refractive index or thickness is retarded differently, and the phase plate turns this phase shift into amplitude (brightness) contrast.

questions.question: In fluorescence microscopy, the light emitted by a fluorophore has a wavelength that is:
questions.explanation: Some energy is lost before emission (the Stokes shift), so emitted light is of longer wavelength, which allows filters to separate it from the excitation light.

questions.question: A confocal microscope rejects out-of-focus light mainly by using:
options: A beam of electrons in a vacuum
A pinhole placed in front of the detector
A pair of crossed polarising filters
Oil with an extremely high refractive index
questions.explanation: The pinhole passes light from the focal plane only, which gives thin optical sections of thick specimens.

questions.question: Polarising microscopy helps distinguish crystalline drug particles from amorphous ones because crystals commonly:
questions.explanation: Anisotropic crystals split polarised light and appear bright against a dark field (birefringence), whereas amorphous solids remain dark.

questions.question: Differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy gives unstained living cells an appearance that is:
options: Shaded and relief-like, as if three-dimensional
Bright structures on a uniformly black background
A thin slice from a single focal plane
questions.explanation: DIC detects gradients in optical path length and renders them as light and dark shading, producing a pseudo-3D relief image.

questions.question: A researcher wants to watch living, unstained, transparent protozoa move while still seeing fine internal structure. The most suitable technique is:
questions.explanation: Phase contrast gives usable contrast in live, unstained transparent cells, whereas the other options require fixing, drying or staining that kills the cells.

questions.question: Living, unstained cells give poor contrast in ordinary bright-field microscopy mainly because they:
options: Absorb very little light, so they are nearly transparent
Have a refractive index far above their surroundings
questions.explanation: Bright-field contrast depends on light absorption, and unstained cells absorb almost none, so there is little difference from the background.

questions.question: The fluorescent dye DAPI is used to label cell nuclei because it binds to:
questions.explanation: DAPI attaches to DNA and fluoresces blue under ultraviolet excitation, so nuclei stand out.

questions.question: Ordinary light microscopes cannot resolve detail much finer than about 0.2 µm mainly because of:
options: The poor quality of glass lenses
Diffraction of light, tied to its wavelength
questions.explanation: Diffraction spreads each point into an Airy disc whose size depends on wavelength and NA, so very close points merge. Lens quality, eyepiece power and chromatic aberration are not the fundamental limit.

questions.question: Which step of the Gram stain causes Gram-negative cells to lose the primary stain?
questions.explanation: The decolouriser (alcohol or acetone) dissolves the outer membrane and washes the crystal violet–iodine complex out of the thin peptidoglycan layer of Gram-negative cells.

questions.question: Pink-red cells after the Gram stain indicate cell walls that:
options: Hold crystal violet in a thick peptidoglycan layer
Contain mycolic acids that bind carbol fuchsin
Lose crystal violet because of thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane
Are covered by a capsule that blocks every dye
questions.explanation: Cells that lose the primary stain because of thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane are recoloured by the safranin counterstain and appear pink-red.

questions.question: Mycobacterium tuberculosis resists decolourisation by acid-alcohol in the Ziehl–Neelsen stain because its wall is rich in:
questions.explanation: The waxy mycolic acid layer holds carbol fuchsin once it has been driven in with heat, making the cells acid-fast.

questions.question: Heat-fixing a bacterial smear mainly serves to:
options: Increase the refractive index of the cells
Enlarge the cells for easier measurement
Dissolve the cell wall so that dye enters
Kill the cells and attach them firmly to the slide
questions.explanation: Fixation kills the cells and adheres them to the glass so they are not washed away during staining.

questions.question: In a negative stain such as India ink or nigrosin, the organism appears:
options: Uniformly dark with a bright halo
questions.explanation: The acidic stain is repelled by the negatively charged cell surface, so it colours the background and leaves the cell clear against a dark background.

questions.question: A hanging-drop preparation is mainly used to observe:
options: The Gram reaction of bacterial walls
questions.explanation: The drop keeps the organisms alive and free to swim, so true motility can be distinguished from Brownian movement.

questions.question: Haematoxylin in an H&E stain colours cell nuclei blue-purple because it behaves as a:
options: Basic dye that binds acidic nucleic acids
Acidic dye that binds basic cytoplasmic proteins
Lipid-soluble dye that dissolves in membranes
questions.explanation: In its mordanted form haematoxylin carries a positive charge and binds the negatively charged phosphate groups of DNA and RNA — it is a basic dye that binds acidic nucleic acids.

questions.question: Giemsa-stained thin blood films are used in malaria diagnosis to visualise:
options: Plasmodium parasites inside red blood cells
questions.explanation: Giemsa stains parasite chromatin and cytoplasm in contrasting colours, so intracellular Plasmodium stages are seen against the red cells.

questions.question: In the Schaeffer–Fulton endospore stain, which result is expected for a Bacillus smear?
options: Green vegetative cells containing red spores
Red vegetative cells and red spores
Green spores within pink vegetative cells
questions.explanation: Heat drives malachite green into the resistant spores, which then hold it, while the vegetative cells are decolourised and take up the safranin counterstain — green spores in pink vegetative cells.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes SEM from TEM?
options: SEM scans a surface to build a topographic image, whereas TEM sends electrons through ultrathin sections
SEM images only through ultrathin sections, whereas TEM scans surfaces
Both use visible photons and differ only in lens quality
SEM operates at atmospheric pressure, whereas TEM requires vacuum
questions.explanation: SEM detects secondary electrons from a scanned surface, whereas TEM detects electrons transmitted through a very thin specimen; both need vacuum.

questions.question: An electron microscope column is held under high vacuum mainly because:
options: Electrons are absorbed by visible light
Vacuum raises the numerical aperture of the lenses
Air molecules would scatter the electron beam
Vacuum stops the magnetic lenses from overheating
questions.explanation: Collisions with gas molecules would deflect and scatter the electron beam, ruining the beam and the image.

questions.question: Electron microscopes resolve far finer detail than light microscopes chiefly because accelerated electrons have:
options: A larger numerical aperture in air
A higher refractive index than photons
questions.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength of accelerated electrons is a small fraction of a nanometre, so the diffraction limit is far shorter than for visible light.

questions.question: The electron beam in a TEM is focused by:
questions.explanation: Electrons are charged, so magnetic fields from electromagnetic coils bend and focus them; glass lenses have no such effect.

questions.question: Uranyl acetate and lead citrate are used in TEM because their heavy atoms:
options: Shorten the wavelength of the electron beam
questions.explanation: Biological material is made of light elements and scatters electrons weakly, so heavy-metal stains scatter electrons strongly and add the density differences needed for contrast.

questions.question: A major limitation of conventional TEM and SEM sample preparation is that it:
options: Needs dehydrated, fixed material, so living cells cannot be viewed
Needs oil immersion, which limits it to bacteria
Cannot detect objects smaller than 0.2 µm
Uses visible light that damages DNA
questions.explanation: Specimens must withstand vacuum and the electron beam, so they are chemically fixed and dehydrated, which kills them.

questions.question: Non-conductive specimens are sputter-coated before SEM with a thin layer of:
questions.explanation: A conductive metal layer (gold or platinum) drains charge and boosts secondary electron emission, avoiding charging artefacts.

questions.question: A TEM micrograph has a scale bar 20 mm long labelled 5 µm. The magnification of the micrograph is:
questions.explanation: Magnification is image length divided by real length: 20 mm0.005 mm = 4000x (since 5 µm = 0.005 mm).

questions.question: Individual virus particles are best examined in structural detail using:
questions.explanation: Most viruses measure about 20–300 nm, which is below the resolution of light microscopes but within that of TEM.

questions.question: A key advantage of cryo-electron microscopy is that it:
options: Removes the need for a vacuum
Allows living cells to be filmed at body temperature
Images biomolecules in a hydrated, near-native state frozen in vitreous ice
Uses visible light with higher aperture
questions.explanation: Rapid freezing preserves molecules in a hydrated, near-native state without dehydration, stains or crystalline ice damage.

questions.question: An eyepiece micrometer is calibrated against a stage micrometer: 100 eyepiece divisions line up with 40 stage divisions, each stage division being 10 µm. One eyepiece division equals:
questions.explanation: 40 stage divisions × 10 µm = 400 µm covers 100 eyepiece divisions, so one eyepiece division = 400 µm100 = 4 µm.

questions.question: At 400x an eyepiece micrometer is calibrated so that one division equals 2.5 µm. A granule spans 18 divisions. Its diameter is:
questions.explanation: Diameter = 18 divisions × 2.5 µm per division = 45 µm.

questions.question: Treating a powdered plant drug with phloroglucinol and concentrated hydrochloric acid turns which structures red-pink?
questions.explanation: Phloroglucinol–HCl reacts with the aldehyde groups of lignin, which identifies lignified vessels and fibres in powdered drugs.

questions.question: Dilute iodine solution applied to a powdered plant drug colours starch grains:
questions.explanation: Iodine forms an inclusion complex with the amylose component of starch, giving a characteristic blue-black colour.

questions.question: Optical microscopy used for particle-size analysis of a suspension is limited chiefly because it:
options: Cannot detect particles larger than 1 µm
Counts only particles that have dissolved
Gives two-dimensional projections and counts relatively few particles
questions.explanation: The method measures projected area diameter in a plane and only a modest number of particles, which can misrepresent three-dimensional shape and the true distribution.

questions.question: After using the 100x oil-immersion objective, the appropriate way to clean it is by:
options: Wiping gently with lens tissue and approved cleaner
Leaving the oil to dry on the lens
questions.explanation: Lens tissue with a suitable cleaning fluid removes oil without scratching the delicate coated lens surface. Water (A) and paper towels (C) can damage the lens, and leaving oil to dry (D) hardens it.
